items.claim: Subtracting the local timezone offset unconditionally breaks server-supplied dates (UTC-midnight ms timestamps) in UTC-negative timezones, showing the previous day.
items.consequence: Python `DatePicker(value=date(2019, 9, 20))` serializes to 1568937600000 (UTC midnight, per `convert_datetime_type`). With a browser in America/Los_Angeles or America/New_York, the offset shift moves it to 2019-09-19T16:00Z, so the picker initially shows Thu Sep 19 2019. The old code showed Sep 20. Reproduced in node with TZ set; an ISO string '2019-09-20' fails the same way. The fix moves the off-by-one from UTC+ users after a click to UTC- users on initial render.

items.claim: `min_date` and `max_date` go through the same shifted `_unlocal_date`, so the selectable range moves one day earlier in UTC-negative timezones.
items.consequence: `DatePicker(min_date=date(2019, 9, 1), max_date=date(2019, 9, 30))` viewed in US timezones: Pikaday gets minDate Aug 31 and maxDate Sep 29. The user can pick Aug 31, which is below the allowed minimum, and cannot pick Sep 30, the allowed maximum. Unlike `value`, these bounds are never rewritten client-side, so they stay wrong on every re-render.

items.claim: For values carrying a time of day, the result is now the browser-local calendar date of the instant, not the date the user gave, so it rolls forward a day in UTC+ zones and back a day in UTC- zones.
items.consequence: `value=datetime(2019, 9, 20, 23, 30)` or `max_date=datetime.utcnow()` late in the UTC day, viewed in Europe/Paris: 23:30Z plus 2h gives Sat Sep 21 2019 (old code: Sep 20 everywhere). `datetime(2019, 9, 20, 0, 30)` viewed in New York gives Sep 19. Both reproduced in node. The displayed date and bounds now depend on the viewer's timezone.

items.claim: The fix is at the wrong depth: `_on_select` stores a local-time `toDateString()` while Python sends UTC-midnight timestamps, and one `_unlocal_date` transform cannot be right for both encodings.
items.consequence: `model.value` alternates between 'Mon Sep 16 2019' (parsed as local midnight) and 1568937600000 (UTC midnight). The old code was right only for the UTC form; the new code is right only for the local form. Whichever is chosen, one path is a day off on one side of UTC. The root fix is to make `_on_select` write a UTC-consistent value (e.g. `Date.UTC(y, m, d)` or 'YYYY-MM-DD' built from local getters) and keep the original UTC-based `_unlocal_date`, or to branch on string versus number input.

items.claim: The new tests do not exercise the bug being fixed and never assert the initially displayed date, so they pass with or without the fix on a UTC machine and miss the UTC- regression.
items.consequence: In a UTC browser (assumed for CI, not checked), `_unlocal_date` is the identity before and after the patch, so `assert el.get_attribute('value') == 'Mon Sep 16 2019'` passes on the unfixed code too. No test checks that the input shows 'Fri Sep 20 2019' right after load, and none runs under a non-UTC TZ. Reverting the fix, or the Sep 19 display in US timezones, leaves the suite green.

items.claim: `_unlocal_date` now mutates its `Date` argument in place via `date.setTime(...)`, a hidden side effect in a function that looks like a pure conversion.
items.consequence: Current callers pass a throwaway `new Date(...)`, so nothing breaks today. Any future caller that passes a Date it keeps (a cached min or max, or a Pikaday `getDate()` result) gets it silently shifted by the timezone offset, and a second call shifts it again. Computing `new Date(date.getTime() - offset)` locally avoids this.

items.claim: The tests use the non-deterministic `max_date=datetime.utcnow()` and copy-paste the same DatePicker construction three times.
items.consequence: The upper bound changes on every run and carries a time of day, which hits the day-rollover path in `_unlocal_date` depending on run time and browser timezone. That makes the max-date behaviour unreproducible and untested. The construction is duplicated on lines 43, 53 and 78; a fixed `max_date=date(2019, 9, 30)` in a shared helper would be deterministic and let the bounds be asserted.

items.claim: `test_server_on_change_round_trip` omits the `page.has_no_console_errors()` check the other two tests make, and does not check the displayed input after the server round trip.
items.consequence: A JS error raised while re-rendering the picker after the server-side `on_change`, or a wrong displayed date after the round trip, goes unnoticed. The test only inspects the timestamps recorded in the ColumnDataSource.
